channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: MIA Watchlist: Track the new US tariffs taking effect on 60-plus partners, Canada's 19 August 50% tariff deadline, whether the Houthi Red Sea blockade holds oil above USD 100, Xi's 24 September US visit, and the ECB's next move.
item.description:
• New US tariffs take effect: the 10–12.5% Section 301 duties on 60-plus partners apply from 24 July, with goods in transit exempt until 28 July — watch for legal challenges and retaliation.
  • Canada's 19 August deadline: the threatened 50% tariff on 500-plus categories lands on 19 August unless Ottawa and Washington reach a deal; Canada has signalled possible retaliation.
  • Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb: whether the Houthi Red Sea blockade holds and the Iran war escalates further will decide if oil stays above USD 100.
  • US–China summit: Xi's 24 September US visit and Beijing's tariff-cut consultation will show whether the managed thaw survives the parallel technology crackdown.
  • ECB's next move: markets are pricing two more rate hikes by year-end; the September meeting is the next test of how the war's energy shock feeds into inflation.

item.title: South Korea and Indonesia posted better-than-expected second-quarter growth, Thailand drew a surge of AI-driven investment, and South Korea and Taiwan now make up more than half of the main emerging-markets index.
item.description:
South Korea's economy grew 0.6% quarter-on-quarter and 3.7% year-on-year in the second quarter, beating forecasts as a semiconductor export boom offset weak construction investment. Indonesia's finance minister expects around 5.4% growth for the quarter and sees momentum strengthening in the second half. Thailand's foreign and domestic investment applications jumped 37% in the first half to USD 43.6 billion, led by a wave of capital into digital infrastructure and AI data centres, cementing its role as a preferred Southeast Asian base. The AI theme is also reshaping portfolios: South Korea and Taiwan together now account for more than 50% of the MSCI Emerging Markets Index, with Taiwan alone at 27% — more than double India's weight. In India, commentators argued a "second wave" of reforms is needed to sustain high growth, while equity strategists see the country benefiting from supply-chain realignment.

Industry Impact

The strength is concentrated in semiconductors, data centres and AI-linked manufacturing — end-markets that consume specialty adhesives, encapsulants and coatings — signalling where materials demand is expanding even as Western construction and autos stagnate. Thailand's investment surge and Southeast Asia's rise as a manufacturing base point to where new production capacity, and its material needs, will land. For a global supplier, the pattern reinforces the case for weighting growth toward AI-exposed Asian industrial hubs.

CNA | Kompas | AP | South China Morning Post | Business Standard

item.title: Spain declared a national emergency over out-of-control wildfires near Madrid, deadly floods disrupted India and Pakistan, and the World Bank put the damage from June's twin earthquakes in Venezuela at USD 19.6 billion.
item.description:
Spain declared an emergency in the Madrid region and Avila as multiple fires burned simultaneously, evacuating more than 10,000 people and handing the response to a military emergency unit; the fires had spread from neighbouring Toledo. In India, torrential rain battered Gujarat and Maharashtra, killing at least one person, prompting some 1,200 rescues and cutting rail links between Gujarat and Mumbai, with premium services cancelled; flooding also damaged power infrastructure in Jammu and Kashmir. In Pakistan, floods in Gilgit-Baltistan washed away roads and bridges and stranded thousands. Further afield, the World Bank estimated USD 19.6 billion in direct damage from Venezuela's June twin earthquakes, which killed more than 5,000 people, with housing accounting for nearly half the loss. A separate study found June's UK heat wave cost the economy GBP 1.15 billion in lost working hours.

Industry Impact

Concentrated natural disasters disrupt regional demand, logistics and construction activity, and the mounting reconstruction bills — nearly USD 20 billion in Venezuela alone — point to future demand for building materials, sealants and protective coatings. Recurrent extreme heat and flooding also raise operating costs and business-continuity risks for plants and supply chains, reinforcing why climate resilience is becoming a standing cost factor rather than an occasional disruption for industrial producers.

The Straits Times | Xinhua | The Times of India | The Standard | Financial Post

item.title: A Bain automotive expert called mergers and alliances the only viable path for a stalling industry, as US light-vehicle sales fell and Chinese brands reached a record share of Europe's market in the first half of 2026.
item.description:
The industry is in what the Bain partner described as its first-ever condition of global stagnation, driven mainly by China's sharp slowdown from double-digit growth to 1–2% and by fierce price competition eroding margins. The numbers bear it out. US light-vehicle sales fell 1.9% in the first half to 6.95 million units, with pure-electric sales down 24% even as hybrids sold well. In Europe, overall registrations rose in the half, but the standout was China: Chinese brands hit a record 10.9% of Europe's new-car market in June and a combined 9.3% share across the EU in the first half, up from 6% a year earlier, led by fast-growing hybrids and plug-in hybrids. Southeast Asia's EV market is also shifting from boosting sales toward building domestic manufacturing, with Vietnam and Thailand positioned to benefit.

Industry Impact

Automotive is a major end-market for adhesives, coatings and sealants, so structural stagnation and consolidation reshape the customer base a supplier depends on. Mergers concentrate purchasing power and can squeeze material suppliers, while the rise of Chinese brands moves specification decisions toward Chinese platforms and standards. The strength of hybrids over pure EVs, and the pivot toward local manufacturing in Southeast Asia, signal where future material demand — and production footprints — are most likely to grow.

La Repubblica | China Economic Net | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | Bizhub

item.title: EU states agreed a scaled-back 21st sanctions package targeting Russian energy, finance and the Moscow Exchange, as Russian strikes halted shipping at Ukraine's Odesa ports for the first time since 2023 and forced Kazakhstan to cut oil output.
item.description:
After weeks of internal wrangling, the EU approved its 21st package since the 2022 invasion, freezing the oil price cap and hitting energy, financial services, crypto and trade; it adds the Moscow Exchange and some 93 Russian banks and institutions to the sanctions list. On the ground, the export picture worsened: no vessels entered any of the three Odesa-region ports as Russia attacked civilian cargo ships in the Black Sea, prompting Maersk to suspend operations at one port and Ukraine to warn that global food security is again at risk for Africa, Asia, the Middle East and Latin America. The disruption also reached energy flows — Kazakhstan temporarily cut oil production because of security problems at the Caspian Pipeline Consortium's Novorossiysk terminal, repeatedly hit by Ukrainian drone strikes.

Industry Impact

The combination of tighter sanctions and physical attacks on Black Sea logistics adds to the energy and commodity uncertainty already driven by the Iran war. Interrupted Kazakh oil flows and blocked grain corridors feed into feedstock and freight costs and into food-price inflation that erodes European consumer demand. For chemicals, the message is that a second conflict theatre continues to disrupt the raw-material and shipping environment, compounding rather than offsetting the Middle East shock.

Daily Sabah | Forbes Russia | Politico Europe | Wallstreet:online

item.title: The yen fell to around 163 per dollar, a level unseen in about 39 years, as investors reacted to the new government's big-spending fiscal plans and the Middle East war, while accelerating inflation strengthens the case for Bank of Japan rate rises.
item.description:
The sell-off follows Prime Minister Takaichi's expansionary "big-boned" fiscal policy, which has unsettled markets worried about Japan's debt trajectory; the Middle East conflict added to the pressure by driving safe-haven dollar buying. Core inflation, excluding fresh food, rose to 1.6% in June and headline inflation to 1.7%, driven largely by energy costs, with a weaker yen threatening to push up imported food and durable-goods prices — a mix that supports the BOJ continuing its exit from ultra-easy policy, though a move may wait until later in the year. The real economy is still expanding: the flash manufacturing PMI held at 54.7 in July with output rising at its fastest pace since 2014, and the composite index stayed above 50 for a 16th straight month. The cabinet's new fiscal guidelines also cited NATO defence-spending benchmarks, pledging to strengthen defence capabilities within five years.

Industry Impact

A weaker yen cuts both ways for chemicals: it makes Japanese exports and locally made materials more competitive abroad, but raises the cost of imported feedstock and energy for producers operating in Japan. Firm factory output signals resilient industrial demand in a key Asian market, while the prospect of BOJ tightening adds another variable to global rate and currency planning. The defence-spending pledge points to sustained demand for advanced materials tied to Japan's rearmament.

The Mainichi | Hong Kong Economic Times | MarketScreener | Global Times

item.title: The ifo Institute expects only 185,000 homes to be completed in Germany this year, the lowest in over a decade, as high building costs and the war hold back a sector already short of well over a million homes.
item.description:
The forecast marks a further decline from around 207,000 completions in 2025 — itself the weakest since 2012 — and points to a construction sector still stuck in crisis rather than recovering. ifo attributes the drop to construction-cost inflation and the economic uncertainty from the Iran war. Any rebound is expected to be very slow, with completions edging up to around 195,000 in 2027 and 210,000 in 2028, held back by the roughly 27 months that now elapse between building approval and handover. The shortfall is acute: Germany is estimated to lack about 1.4 million homes, concentrated in its major cities, so the weak pipeline compounds a structural housing shortage rather than merely reflecting a cyclical dip.

Industry Impact

Residential construction is a core end-market for adhesives, sealants and coatings, so a completions figure at a multi-year low directly limits volume in Germany, Europe's largest construction market. The extended approval-to-handover lag means the weakness is locked in for the next two to three years regardless of demand, giving suppliers little near-term relief. It reinforces the case for tilting toward renovation, infrastructure and nearshored industrial construction, where activity is holding up better than new housing.

Die Zeit | Tagesschau

item.title: The US House voted to bar Chinese humanoid robots from military use, a Senate panel advanced a tougher ban on Chinese automakers, and US officials accused China's Moonshot of stealing American technology to build its latest AI model.
item.description:
The defence policy bill would stop the Pentagon from buying, leasing or operating humanoid robots linked to China, Russia or Iran, extending restrictions on foreign autonomous systems. The Senate Commerce Committee approved a bill tightening the ban on Chinese automakers; a provision barring firms more than 15% Chinese-owned would catch Mercedes-Benz, given its roughly 20% passive Chinese stake, with compliance required by 2030. Separately, a senior White House tech official accused Moonshot AI of using American technology — including a distilled US model and advanced Nvidia chips — to build its Kimi K3 model, and the Treasury is weighing sanctions and a trade blacklist. On the other side of the race, Japan's industry ministry set a target of 10 million AI robots across 18 sectors by 2040, backed by JPY 1 trillion over five years to offset a projected shortage of 3.39 million specialists.

Industry Impact

The hardening technology split matters to chemicals through its customers: automakers, electronics and robotics firms are being forced to pick sides and reorganise supply chains, which reshapes where advanced materials, adhesives and coatings are specified. The Mercedes provision shows how ownership rules can suddenly threaten market access for a major coatings customer. Japan's robot push, meanwhile, signals durable demand for the specialty materials that automation hardware requires.

SCMP | The Standard | The Independent | POLITICO | Forbes Japan

item.title: Even as new trade measures mount, President Trump said Xi Jinping will visit the US on 24 September, and Beijing began consulting industry on a framework to cut tariffs on about USD 30 billion of two-way trade.
item.description:
The two developments point to a managed thaw running in parallel with the tariff escalation elsewhere. Trump said artificial intelligence would be high on the agenda for the September talks, framing AI competition as central to the relationship. On the same day, China's Commerce Ministry said it is gathering views from local governments, businesses and associations on reciprocal tariff-cut arrangements — including agricultural products — under a trade board the two sides agreed to set up earlier in 2026, with the aim of finalising and implementing specific product lists quickly. Hong Kong media reported Xi may stop in Canada en route to avoid appearing overly pro-US; it would be his first visit there as leader. The diplomacy coexists uneasily with Washington's tightening measures on Chinese robots, vehicles and AI.

Industry Impact

A concrete summit date and a live tariff-cut process are the clearest signs yet that the world's two largest economies want to cap, not deepen, their trade conflict — a modest positive for globally exposed chemicals demand. But the narrow USD 30 billion scope and the simultaneous technology crackdown show the détente is tactical. Producers should treat any relief as partial and reversible, and keep planning around a structurally divided US-China market.

Il Sole 24 Ore | The Standard | Chinatimes

item.title: A German court ruled reusable carrier bags count as packaging, subjecting retailers to recycling fees, as US and UK chemical rules tighten — while coatings maker VIP Coatings expanded into Central and Eastern Europe on the nearshoring wave.
item.description:
Germany's Federal Administrative Court sided with the packaging register against retailer Rewe, confirming that durable plastic bags are packaging and that sellers must fund their recycling — a precedent that widens producer-responsibility obligations. In the US, some 250 public-health and environmental groups urged the Senate to reject industry efforts to weaken the Toxic Substances Control Act, the main federal chemicals law. In Britain, the Environment Agency flagged catchment reviews to 2035 that could force abstraction cuts affecting the up-to-50% of chemical firms that draw water from surface sources and boreholes. Circular-economy activity is also picking up, with Clearwater Paper launching fully recycled packaging board in the US and SK Chemicals seeking partners to recycle waste banners. Against this regulatory tightening, Germany's VIP Coatings is bringing polyaspartic, polyurethane and polyurea technologies to Poland and Romania to serve fast-growing nearshored industrial assets.

Industry Impact

This cluster maps directly onto the adhesives, coatings and sealants business. Extended producer-responsibility and recycling rules raise compliance costs across the packaging value chain, while tighter chemicals regulation and water-abstraction limits touch both formulations and plant operations. The bright spot is demand: Europe's nearshoring boom is creating new industrial assets that need high-performance coatings, offering a growth channel that partly offsets the regulatory and cost pressure building elsewhere.

Handelsblatt | AP | AP | CIA | MarketScreener

item.title: The European Central Bank kept its benchmark rate at 2.25%, pausing after June's hike to judge how volatile energy prices will affect inflation, while German bond yields rose to their highest level since 2011.
item.description:
June's quarter-point rise — the first since 2023 — was aimed at containing inflation from the oil spike caused by the US-Iran war and the Hormuz disruption. This time the ECB chose to wait, wary of choking off an already sluggish euro-zone recovery even as fighting resumed and oil climbed back toward USD 100. President Lagarde said risks to growth are tilted to the downside, warning that fresh energy-supply shocks could keep prices elevated longer than expected and weigh on incomes, spending and investment. Markets read the pause as temporary: German ten-year yields rose to 3.21%, a 15-year high, and investors are now fully pricing two more quarter-point hikes by year-end. Lagarde separately dismissed speculation about an early exit, saying she will not leave before her term ends in October 2027, despite talk linking her to French politics.

Industry Impact

A steady policy rate offers short-term predictability for financing and hedging, but the market's bet on two more hikes signals that European borrowing costs are more likely to rise than fall. For capital-intensive chemicals producers, that keeps the cost of funding new capacity high just as demand in construction and manufacturing remains weak. The downside growth warning is the more important message: the ECB sees the war's energy shock, not a recovery, as the dominant risk to the European customer base.

AP | Le Figaro | Il Sole 24 Ore | Handelsblatt

item.title: Alongside the broad new duties, Washington threatened a 50% tariff on over 500 categories of Canadian goods from 19 August, prompting Prime Minister Carney to say "everything is on the table" while both sides agree to intensify talks.
item.description:
The 50% tariff, applied under Section 338, would hit around USD 20 billion of exports — about 5% of Canada's 2025 shipments to the US — and cover goods from cement and wood products to spirits, perfumes and candles, while sparing energy. Economists expect it to shave two to three tenths of a percentage point off Canadian growth in 2026 and 2027 without tipping the country into recession. Canada's electronics sector is seen as among the hardest hit, with production integrated across the border. Carney has not ruled out federal or provincial countermeasures and has agreed with Trump to step up negotiations before the deadline. Separately, US Trade Representative Greer said he aims for interim deals with Canada and Mexico by year-end, with deeper USMCA changes pushed into 2027; Washington has signalled it will not renew the pact on its old terms.

Industry Impact

The named categories include cement and wood products, placing construction-linked materials — adjacent to the adhesives, coatings and sealants used in building — squarely in scope. For suppliers with integrated North American operations, a 50% wall forces a rethink of where to produce and stock. Canada and China remain among the few partners actively retaliating, so escalation risk is real, and the uncertainty over USMCA's future terms complicates any medium-term investment decision on the continent.

The Globe and Mail | Los Angeles Times | Financial Post | BNN Bloomberg

item.title: Brent briefly passed USD 100 for the first time in nearly two months after new US strikes on Iran and Houthi attacks on Saudi tankers threatened to disrupt Red Sea shipping alongside the near-closed Strait of Hormuz.
item.description:
The war, now in its second phase, has already idled traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. The new escalation came when Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis declared a blockade of Bab el-Mandeb to Saudi-linked shipping and struck two tankers, retaliating for Saudi Arabia's blockade of rebel-held Yemen. Bab el-Mandeb carries roughly 12% of world trade and a quarter of container traffic between Europe and Asia via the Suez Canal, so a second closed chokepoint magnifies the shock. At least seven ships have already rerouted, though a Chinese tanker was reportedly allowed through case by case. Brent, which had fallen to around USD 70 in early July, climbed to USD 98–100 before easing slightly. The disruption is rippling outward: Indian airlines have cancelled some 26,000 flights over Middle East airspace closures, and ASEAN diplomats have openly criticised Washington for underestimating the regional fallout.

Industry Impact

Oil above USD 100 feeds directly into petrochemical feedstock, energy and freight costs across the chemicals value chain, squeezing margins on adhesives, coatings and sealants that are already energy-intensive to produce. A second blocked chokepoint lengthens Europe–Asia shipping routes and raises the risk of raw-material delays, on top of higher marine insurance. The combination of costlier energy and stretched logistics is exactly the environment in which producers lose pricing power to volatile input costs.

Lianhe Zaobao | CNA | AP | Handelsblatt | POLITICO

item.title: The US let its temporary 10% import tariff expire and immediately replaced it with new 10–12.5% duties on more than 60 trading partners, covering 99.4% of imports and justified by weak enforcement against forced labour.
item.description:
The temporary 10% tariff, imposed in February 2026, was struck down by the Supreme Court earlier this year, forcing the administration to find a new legal basis. It turned to Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act and a forced-labour investigation opened in March. Around ten partners judged to have adequate rules — including Canada, Mexico, the UK, the EU and India — face 10%, while some 43 others such as Japan, China and South Korea face 12.5%. Food, fuel and fertiliser are exempt, as are steel, aluminium, cars and pharmaceuticals already covered by separate tariffs, and USMCA-compliant goods. The new duties have no legal ceiling and last at least four years, making them more durable than the measure they replace. This follows recent 25% tariffs on Brazil and 100–200% on generic drugs, and Washington is also probing 16 partners for excess manufacturing capacity, signalling more to come.

Industry Impact

For a chemicals group, the shift from a temporary blanket tariff to durable, sector-specific duties means tariff exposure is now a permanent planning variable rather than a passing shock. The exemption for steel, aluminium, cars and pharma limits direct input-cost pain, but the breadth — covering nearly all imports — raises the cost and complexity of transatlantic and trans-Pacific supply chains. The capacity probe is the more worrying signal, as it could eventually reach chemicals and reshape where customers site production.

Bloomberg | Politico | Handelsblatt | The Guardian | The Straits Times

item.title: MIA Digest: The US replaced its expired blanket tariff with durable 10-12.5% duties on 60-plus partners, oil topped USD 100 as the Iran war reached the Red Sea, and the ECB held rates while Xi confirmed a September US visit.
item.description:
• Tariff wall rebuilt: the expired 10% tariff was replaced overnight by new Section 301 duties of 10-12.5% on 60-plus partners, covering 99.4% of US imports, with a separate 50% threat on Canada.
  • Oil past USD 100: Brent briefly cleared USD 100 for the first time in two months as Houthi attacks opened a second shipping chokepoint at Bab el-Mandeb.
  • Central banks wait: the ECB held at 2.25% to gauge the war's energy shock, while German bond yields hit a 15-year high.
  • US-China both ways: Beijing consulted on cutting tariffs and Xi confirmed a 24 September US visit, even as Washington moved against Chinese robots, cars and AI.
  • Chemicals in focus: a German court widened packaging-recycling duties and UK and US chemical regulation tightened, while coatings demand grew on European nearshoring.
